newsitem.title: UK: Ernest Saunders says UK conviction was unfair.
newsitem.headline: Ernest Saunders says UK conviction was unfair.

text.p: Former Guinness chairman Ernest Saunders said on Tuesday he believed he would have been acquitted of fraud charges if evidence found by the European Court of Human Rights to have been unfairly obtained, had not been allowed at his trial.
"My impression is that if the evidence had not been used I would have been acquitted," Saunders told reporters at a briefing following news of the Strasbourg court's ruling.
"This is just the tip of the iceberg of a politically managed and totally unfair process. The government should not be allowed to manipulate the legal process for its own political agenda," he added.
The European court ruled that Britain had denied Saunders, who was convicted of fraud in 1990, a fair trial.

Saunders, now 61, was convicted in 1990 on 12 counts including false accounting and theft for inflating Guinness' share price to help its 1986 takeover of whisky group Distillers Plc prevail against rival bidder Argyll Plc.

Saunders said he would be considering all his options in the wake of the ruling and confirmed he would be considering a third appeal to the Court of Appeal. Such a move would have to be referred to the court by Britain's home secretary.

He said it was sufficient that he had won the case on the point of principle. His claim for 4.6 million stg in compensation for lost earnings was rejected but the UK government was ordered to pay him 75,000 stg in legal costs.
